title: Replace worn carbon brushes in a motor
summary: Brushed motors in drills, grinders, vacuums, blenders, treadmills and car parts stop when their carbon brushes wear down. Replacing or re-shaping brushes and cleaning the commutator brings most of them back.

materials.item: Replacement carbon brushes, or larger brushes from a donor motor filed to fit
Donor brushed motor for brushes and springs

steps.text: Know the signs: the motor runs on and off, only runs in some positions, sparks a lot, smells hot, or is weak. Brushes are the first thing to check.
Unplug the tool or disconnect its battery.
steps.warn: Mains motors carry full mains voltage at the brushes. Never work on them plugged in.

steps.text: Find the brush holders. Many corded tools have two screw caps on opposite sides of the motor body. Others need the case opened; the brushes sit in small holders pressing on the copper commutator at the back of the motor.
Take out each brush with its spring. Mark which way round it came out: the curved face matches the commutator.
steps.warn: Brush springs flick out. Hold a thumb over the holder as you release them.

steps.text: Measure the brushes. Replace them when they are worn to about a third of their new length or past any wear line. Some brushes have a plastic pin that stops the motor when they are worn; those must be replaced.

Look at the commutator: the ring of copper bars the brushes ride on. Smooth and brown is normal. Clean black or rough areas with fine sandpaper held on a stick while turning the motor by hand. Pick dirt out of the gaps between bars with a knife point. Blow out the dust.
Fit the new brushes. If they are oversized, file the sides until each slides freely in its holder without rocking.
Shape a new brush face: wrap sandpaper around the commutator, rough side out, and turn the motor back and forth with the brush pressed on it until the face is curved to match.
Refit the springs and connect the brush leads (clip, screw or solder) exactly as they were.
Run the motor with no load for 5–10 minutes so the brushes bed in. Small blue sparks at the brushes are normal. A ring of orange sparks means the commutator is damaged or the brushes don't fit.

notes:
## Brush types matter

- **Mains motors** (drills, grinders, vacuums, blenders) use carbon or graphite brushes with fairly high resistance to keep sparking down.
- **Low-voltage high-current motors** (starter motors, cordless tools, some 12 V motors) use copper-graphite brushes: shiny, coppery, low resistance.

Swapping one type for the other works poorly: copper brushes in a mains motor wear the commutator and spark; carbon brushes in a starter motor drop too much voltage.

## Improvising brushes

- File larger brushes from another motor down to size. This is the best field fix.
- Carbon rods from old zinc-carbon batteries can be filed into brushes for small low-power motors. They are harder than real brushes and wear the commutator faster: a stopgap only.

## When it isn't the brushes

- Burnt smell and dark windings: the armature or field is burnt out.
- Commutator bars lifted, burnt through or very worn: needs a lathe to skim, or a new armature.
- A motor that hums but won't turn is often seized bearings or gears.

## Where brushes are found

Every corded drill, angle grinder, circular saw, vacuum, blender and older washing machine; treadmill motors; car starters, alternators, wiper and window motors; brushed cordless tools. Spare brush sets are often taped inside tool cases or sold in hardware stores.
